summary: Defines a MIB module of textual conventions for MPLS management information, so that other MPLS MIB modules can import them instead of defining their own. It was updated by RFC 7274.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3811 defines shared data types for describing Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) network information in management modules. Reusing the same definitions helps those modules interpret labels, identifiers, rates, and tunnel settings consistently.

subtitle: Reusable MIB data types for managing MPLS labels, paths, and tunnels.

tldr.problem: MPLS management modules need consistent ways to represent labels, rates, paths, and tunnel details. Defining these data types separately can create incompatible descriptions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3811 defines the MPLS-TC-STD-MIB module, which contains textual conventions for other MPLS MIB modules to import.
tldr.outcome: The shared conventions cover MPLS management values. RFC 3811 was later updated by RFC 7274.

today: RFC 3811 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 7274. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Purpose of the MPLS Conventions
sections.content:
The MPLS-TC-STD-MIB module collects textual conventions for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) management information. Other MPLS MIB modules should import these conventions instead of defining their own versions.

The module follows Structure of Management Information version 2 (SMIv2) and defines types only; it does not define managed objects. MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is a shared vocabulary for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) management data. Other management modules can reuse the definitions to record the same kinds of values consistently.

sections.title: Rates, Burst Sizes, and Labels
sections.content:
MplsBitRate records bandwidth in units of 1,000 bits per second, rounded to the nearest 1,000. A value of zero means the traffic is treated as best effort. MplsBurstSize records how many octets may be sent back-to-back without concern for policing; zero means burst size is unsupported.

MplsLabel can represent labels used by different MPLS technologies. A label in an MPLS shim header is a 20-bit value carried in 4 octets, with the remaining bits required to be zero. The convention also describes reserved values and label forms for Frame Relay, ATM, and GMPLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The module gives management systems consistent ways to record bandwidth, burst size, and MPLS labels. Some label values are reserved, and the format depends on the technology carrying the label.

sections.title: Router, Path, and Tunnel Identifiers
sections.content:
An MplsLdpIdentifier is six octets: the first four identify a Label Switching Router, and the last two identify a label space within that router. MplsLSPID identifies a Label Switched Path and has a size of 2 or 6 octets, depending on the signaling protocol.

The module also defines tunnel and path indexes. A tunnel instance index of zero denotes the configured tunnel interface; values above zero can identify signaled or backup instances, while values above 65535 apply to fast-reroute detour instances.
sections.plainLanguage: These conventions describe how management data identifies routers, paths, and tunnel instances. The fields have set formats so that systems can tell which network item each value refers to.

sections.title: Enumerations for MPLS Behavior
sections.content:
Several conventions are enumerations with a fixed set of choices. Examples include downstream-on-demand or downstream-unsolicited label distribution, conservative or liberal label retention, and generic, ATM, or Frame Relay label types.

MplsOwner records which management subsystem originally created an object. TeHopAddressType identifies whether a traffic-engineered tunnel hop is an IPv4 address, IPv6 address, AS number, unnumbered interface, or LSP identifier. Its associated address value must match the selected type.
sections.plainLanguage: Some fields use a short list of named choices. The selected value tells a management system which label behavior, object owner, or tunnel-hop address format applies.

sections.title: Security, IANA, and Status
sections.content:
The module defines no management objects, so the RFC says meaningful security considerations belong in modules that define objects using these conventions. IANA assigned the MPLS MIB subtree under { transmission 166 } and the module beneath it.

RFC 3811 is a Proposed Standard. The batch metadata records that RFC 7274 updates it.
sections.plainLanguage: The conventions themselves do not define managed objects; security review belongs with modules that use them. RFC 7274 later updated this Proposed Standard.
